title: India's $315-Billion IT Empire Faces Its AI Reckoning
excerpt: TCS chairman says AI agents will match headcount. Nifty IT is down 25%. And the outsourcing model that built India's middle class is being rewritten in real time
body:
When the chairman of India's largest IT company tells an annual general meeting that AI agents will soon equal the number of human employees, it's not a prediction. It's a warning shot.

N. Chandrasekaran, chairman of Tata Consultancy Services, made the statement at TCS's AGM this week: "If the company has half a million employees, the day is not far when the company will have half a million AI agents. The company's employees and AI agents will work together, and that will be the future."

The market's verdict has been swift and brutal. TCS shares have fallen more than 32% in 2026. The broader Nifty IT index is down 25%. And the tremors are being felt across India's entire $315-billion information technology sector — an industry that employs millions, drives 80% of the country's services exports, and has, for three decades, served as the primary economic escalator for India's middle class.

## The Numbers Behind the Collapse

The scale of the workforce contraction is already visible. TCS cut more than 12,000 jobs last July. Its net headcount fell by over 23,000 in the fiscal year ended March 2026, leaving the company with 584,519 employees. Across the top three firms — TCS, Infosys, and Wipro — the collective headcount reduction exceeds 42,000 in recent years, even as each has deployed over 50,000 AI licences internally.

The trigger for the latest selloff was Opendoor's decision to shut its India operations entirely, with CEO Carsten Koerl explicitly crediting AI for eliminating the need for offshore operational staff. Venture capitalist Sheel Mohnot of Better Tomorrow Ventures was blunt: "As manual work gets replaced by AI, a lot of jobs will be lost in India."

Keshav Lohia of Emergent Ventures called it a "watershed moment," arguing that AI advances are beginning to challenge the cost-arbitrage model that made India a dominant offshoring destination for over two decades.

## The Structural Threat

The challenge goes beyond cyclical hiring slowdowns. Jefferies, the global investment bank, has warned that AI could reduce revenue growth for Indian IT services firms by up to 3% annually over the next five years — a compounding hit that would fundamentally reshape the industry's economics.

Phil Fersht, chief executive of HFS Research, argues the shift is even more profound. "This is not an isolated restructuring," he told TechCrunch. "It is part of a much broader pattern we are starting to see as companies redesign operations around AI, automation, and much leaner workflows." He describes the emerging model as "services-as-software" — companies delivering outcomes through AI-augmented platforms rather than large human teams.

TCS itself is pivoting aggressively. This week, it announced a partnership with Anthropic — the same company whose AI agent tool launch in February triggered a $62.8 billion wipeout in Indian IT market capitalisation. The alliance will equip 50,000 TCS associates with Anthropic's Claude AI. Rival Infosys struck a similar partnership with Anthropic back in February.

The irony is stark: India's IT giants are partnering with the very companies whose products threaten to make their traditional business model obsolete.

## What This Means for NRI Investors

For the Indian diaspora, the IT sector's convulsions are both financial and personal. NRI investors hold significant positions in Indian IT stocks — Infosys, TCS, Wipro, and HCL Tech are among the most widely held equities in Indian American portfolios. The sector's 25% decline this year represents billions in erosion of diaspora wealth.

But the exposure runs deeper than portfolios. Millions of Indian Americans built their careers in or around IT services. Many maintain family networks in Bengaluru, Hyderabad, Pune, and Chennai that are deeply embedded in the industry's ecosystem. A structural downturn in IT hiring doesn't just affect stock prices — it affects the economic trajectory of an entire generation of young Indians who viewed software engineering as their most reliable path to prosperity.

## The Counter-Argument — and Why It's Insufficient

Not everyone is pessimistic. Microsoft India's executive recently argued that "AI will create more jobs than it disrupts," drawing parallels with the internet revolution of the 1990s. New roles like AI trainers, agent specialists, and AI security experts are indeed emerging. India's Global Capability Centres (GCCs) — in-house tech arms of multinational corporations — now account for 30-35% of AI-related hiring in the country, with demand for AI specialists up more than 300% since 2024.

But the mismatch between the jobs being destroyed and the jobs being created is severe. Entry-level coding positions — the traditional entry point for millions of Indian engineering graduates — are precisely the roles most vulnerable to AI automation. The GCC jobs replacing them require mid-to-senior experience; TeamLease Digital reports that experienced hires rose from 60% of GCC recruitment in 2023 to over 77% in fiscal 2026.

The Quess Corp Q4 FY26 findings paint the supply-side picture starkly: a 38-42% gap exists in AI and data skills across India's GCC ecosystem. India has the demand, but it doesn't yet have the workforce to meet it.

Chandrasekaran insists TCS won't downsize — it will simply hire fewer people. But in an industry that has historically grown by adding headcount, "hiring less" at scale is functionally a contraction. For NRI families with children considering IT careers, the message is unmistakable: the India tech ladder that lifted their parents' generation is being fundamentally restructured, and the rungs at the bottom are disappearing first.
